result.summary: After a truce to burn the dead, the Greeks and Trojans fight again. Neoptolemus and Deiphobus rage across the field until Apollo and Poseidon intervene, and Calchas tells the Greeks that Troy cannot fall without Philoctetes. Ulysses and Diomede bring Philoctetes back from Lemnos, he is healed, reconciled with Agamemnon, and the Greeks march out again.

scenes.title: Antenor's prayer to Zeus
scenes.summary: The Trojans cower, fearing Achilles lives. Antenor begs Zeus to end their suffering, and Zeus grants doom to Troy but keeps Neoptolemus fighting.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans face destruction of their city and people.

scenes.title: Truce and funeral pyres
scenes.summary: Priam asks for a truce to burn the dead. Neoptolemus mourns at Achilles' tomb and returns to the ships with Phoenix.
scenes.stakes: Grief for the fallen and the unmet father.

place.name: Plain of Troy by the Hellespont

scenes.title: Deiphobus rallies Troy
scenes.summary: The Greeks pour out; Deiphobus exhorts the Trojans, who arm amid family farewells and march out to battle while Helen stays hidden.
scenes.stakes: Trojans risk their homes, families and lives.

scenes.title: Deiphobus and Neoptolemus clash
scenes.summary: Deiphobus slaughters Greeks until Neoptolemus, driven by Automedon, confronts him. Apollo hides Deiphobus in cloud, and Neoptolemus rallies the Greeks against the Scaean Gate.
scenes.stakes: Deiphobus risks death at Neoptolemus' spear; Greeks risk slaughter.

place.name: Plain before Troy, Xanthus and Scaean Gate

scenes.title: Gods clash; Calchas advises
scenes.summary: Apollo descends to aid Troy; Poseidon forbids him to kill Neoptolemus. Calchas then declares Philoctetes is needed, and Ulysses and Diomede are sent to Lemnos.
scenes.stakes: Troy's fate and the gods' quarrel; Greek hopes of victory.

scenes.title: Philoctetes found on Lemnos
scenes.summary: After a digression on the Lemnian women, the envoys find Philoctetes wasted by his wound. Athena softens his wrath and he goes with them.
scenes.stakes: Philoctetes risks death by wound and hunger; the envoys risk his arrows.

scenes.title: Healing and reconciliation
scenes.summary: They sail back to the camp, where Podaleirius heals Philoctetes and Athena restores him. Agamemnon apologizes with gifts, and the Greeks arm for battle.
scenes.stakes: Reconciliation of Philoctetes with the Greeks.

alias_notes.explanation: Greek name for Ulysses, used once in this translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Deiphobus' consoling maxim that all things follow the law of change.
Agamemnon's view that no one can escape the Fates or choose his own way.

analysis.text: Fate and divine will govern human affairs: Troy's fall waits on Philoctetes, and Agamemnon excuses the abandonment as the work of the Fates.
The Philoctetes story comes from the lost epic cycle and was also dramatized by Sophocles; Quintus of Smyrna retells it in the Homeric style.

legacy.text: Philoctetes' abandonment and return inspired Sophocles' play Philoctetes (409 BC) and later retellings.

fun_facts.text: The Lemnian women's massacre of their husbands was a famous myth, used here as a brief digression.

language_notes.text: This is the book's heading: it announces how Philoctetes came back to the war after his long, solitary banishment.
Ilium is another name for Troy; its towers stand clear in the morning air.
Thralls means slaves or captives; here the Trojans are gripped by fear as if enslaved.
Antenor does not know whether Achilles is truly alive, so he says 'be he Achilles... or some other like to him.'
Dardanus, son of Zeus, was the ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so Antenor appeals to Zeus's kinship with Troy.
Nereid Queen is Thetis, a sea-goddess and Achilles' mother, whom Zeus will honour through her grandson's fame.
Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles; here it means the shore near it, where the Greek camp lay.
"Gave ear" means they listened and agreed to the request.
"Argives" is another name for the Greeks, as are Achaeans and Danaans.
"Dardanian" means of Dardanus, the ancestor of the Trojans; the Gate is a Trojan city gate.
"Aweless" means fearless, not inspiring awe in others; it describes Achilles' son Neoptolemus.
"Quail" means to shrink in fear.
"Two and ten" is an archaic way of saying twelve.
Firmament means the vault of the sky, the heavens.
"Either did some God... or" means: either a god filled him with courage, or his own spirit drove him. The poet leaves the cause open.
Alexander is another name for Paris, whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
"Ye" is the archaic plural "you"; "shroud me o'er" means may she cover me in death, as the earth of a grave.
Achilles was the greatest Greek warrior; he was killed and his body burned on a pyre, so the Trojans need not fear him.
Achaean is another name for a Greek.
"Waxed" means grew; "Time's changeless law of change" means that change itself is the one constant.
"Cumbered with the reins" means hampered or encumbered by holding the reins, leaving his hands unable to fight.
"Billets overturfed" refers to charcoal-burning: logs stacked and covered with turf, then set smouldering to make charcoal.
"Peleides' fierce-heart son" means the son of Achilles, Peleus' son; Neoptolemus is meant.
"Troyward-fleeing" describes foes running back toward Troy.
"Cronos' Son" is Jove (Zeus), who here lifts the cloud Apollo had made.
"War-blencher" means one who flinches from battle, a coward.
The son of Leto is Apollo, named by his mother, the Titaness Leto; his twin sister is Artemis.
Welkin is an archaic poetic word for the sky or heavens.
The mighty Shaker of Earth is Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes, here siding with the Greeks.
Apollo earlier killed Achilles, Neoptolemus's father, at Troy; 'erst' means formerly.
Birds of boding screamed to left: bird behaviour was read as omens, here warning Apollo against his intended act.
Olympus' Lord is Jove, who would be angry at the death of Achilles' son; the gods' quarrels risk his anger.
Poseidon is brother of Jove, Apollo's father, so he is Apollo's uncle: 'brother of his sire'.
Odysseus here is the same hero the translation elsewhere calls Ulysses; Tydeus' son is Diomede.
The Fire-god is Hephaestus, whose city on Lemnos was Hephaestia. The Lemnian women killed their husbands for preferring Thracian captives, a story told next.
Elf-locks are wild, tangled, matted hair.
"Beetling" means overhanging; "tare" is an old past tense of "tear"; "fell" means deadly.
"His heart's stern will he had swiftly wrought" means he would quickly have carried out his harsh intent, shooting them.
"Hearkening" means listening; "olden wrongs" are his old grievances at being abandoned.
"Hawsers" are mooring ropes, and "anchor-stones" are the stones used as anchors; "dayspring" is dawn.
Stern-sheets are the ropes (sheets) controlling the sail's trim; here both are pulled tight to catch the wind.
Poeas' valiant son is Philoctetes, identified by his father's name; 'bare' means 'bore', i.e. carried.
Trito-born is Athena (Minerva in Latin), called Tritogeneia, an old epithet of uncertain origin linked to the name Triton.
'I trow' means 'I believe'; 'perverted' here means our minds were turned astray by the gods.
A tripod is a three-legged bronze cauldron, a valued prize and gift in Greek society.
'Obdurate' means stubborn; 'rancours' are bitter grudges; 'anon' means soon.
''Gan whet' means 'began to sharpen'; 'foddered' means fed.

context_notes.text: Antenor is a Trojan elder, often counselling peace with the Greeks. Ida is the mountain near Troy associated with Zeus.
Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, who has joined the Greeks and is fighting at Troy.
Eurypylus was an ally of Troy who came to help and was killed in battle by Neoptolemus; Priam treated him almost as a son.
Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, came to Troy after his father's death and had never met him.
Phoenix was Achilles' old tutor and companion. The Myrmidons were Achilles' soldiers, now following his son.
Deiphobus was a son of Priam and brother of Hector and Paris, and became a leading Trojan defender after Hector's death.
Zeus is the king of the gods and sends weather; this translation uses the Greek name here, though it often uses Jove.
Helen, wife of Menelaus, was taken to Troy by Paris. She feels shame as the war rages over her.
Thetis, a sea goddess, was Achilles' mother and so Neoptolemus' grandmother.
Scamander is another name for the river Xanthus near Troy.
Automedon was Achilles' charioteer; the immortal horses were Achilles', now driven for his son.
Phoebus is Apollo, a protector of Troy, who also helped bring about Achilles' death.
Xanthus is the river on the Trojan plain, also called the Scamander.
Calchas was the Greek seer; Philoctetes, heir of Heracles's bow, had been left on Lemnos, and Troy was fated to fall only with his help.
The sons of Atreus are Agamemnon and Menelaus, leaders of the Greek army.
The heroes are Odysseus (called Ulysses elsewhere) and Diomede, sent to fetch Philoctetes, son of Poeas, because Troy cannot fall without his bow.
Hercules gave this bow to Philoctetes in thanks for lighting his funeral pyre. Its arrows are fated to be needed to take Troy.
The Fates were goddesses who spun out each person's destiny, which even gods did not easily change.
Podaleirius, son of Asclepius, was a Greek physician at Troy, like his brother Machaon.
The Greeks had abandoned Philoctetes on Lemnos because of his foul, painful snakebite wound.
Ilium is another name for Troy; Philoctetes' arrows were fated to be needed for its fall.

literary_notes.text: Dawn rising and the air glowing with splendour make a bright, clear picture that contrasts with the Trojans' dread.
Antenor speaks directly to Zeus and reproaches him, which makes the prayer passionate and accusing.
Antenor asks for a quick end to Troy's suffering, and the god grants that destruction, which is a bitter answer to his prayer.
The closing line states a general truth about honoring the dead, justifying the Greeks' mercy in a brief maxim.
Weeping, kissing and embracing the pillar show Neoptolemus' devotion and grief for a father he never knew.
He addresses the dead Achilles directly, as if his father could hear.
The mutual "not seen" stresses the tragedy of father and son who never met, deepening the emotion.
Night, stars and dawn give a calm, cyclical close after the grief and burning of the dead.
The Greeks pouring out are compared to thick, heavy snowflakes, suggesting an overwhelming, silent-seeming mass.
The Trojans' foreboding of doom and the cloud-like enemy hint at the city's eventual fall.
Deiphobus breaks off to address his country directly, showing passionate patriotism.
Storms and calm morning stand for war and peace, comforting the Trojans with nature's cycle.
The father's mixed grief and smiles show how family love hardens his resolve.
Sound and sight pile up, with roaring cries, clanging shields and blood-red armor, to convey the chaos of battle.
Death exults and Strife shrieks, turning abstractions into figures presiding over the battle.
Deiphobus' slaughter is likened to a woodman felling trees, showing his effortless, relentless work and the Greeks falling in heaps.
Fish speared in a net show Greeks helplessly cut down, and the reddened water links the image to the bloodied Xanthus.
The boar caught between fleeing and fighting before a lion conveys Deiphobus' fear and indecision at seeing Neoptolemus.
Neoptolemus is shown as the image of his father, inspiring the same fear Achilles did.
The Trojans' terror is compared to sailors facing a huge wave, and the cloak metaphor adds to it.
Golden armour and lightning-splendour paint Apollo's descent as dazzling light streaking across the sky.
Earth-shaker and Sea-king name Poseidon by his powers, and the quaking ground shows his approach.
Strife is given a body and gloats like a spectator, turning human slaughter into the gods' entertainment.
Calchas is likened to a god in his knowledge of the future, stressing his authority and why the Greeks trust him.
The balanced clauses show the birds feeding and clothing him, summarizing his reliance on his bow.
Philoctetes is compared to a trapped wild animal gnawing off its own limb, stressing his savage, suffering state.
The sea-eaten cliff mirrors the wound slowly gnawing his strength. Enduring stone worn down by waves suggests even a mighty hero can be undone.
Athena abruptly dissolves his wrath, showing the gods steering the plot toward Troy's fall.
The half-felled tree, groaning and propped on remaining wood, vividly compares Philoctetes' weakened body leaning on his supporters.
Revived grain after storm and warm wind pictures Philoctetes' sudden return to health.
Men drifting like wind-driven leaves expresses human helplessness before fate, a Homeric image.
The claim of no gap between men stresses the army's tight, formidable unity.
